newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says no change is planned in forex regime.
newsitem.headline: Israel says no change is planned in forex regime.

text.p: Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Tuesday that they planned no changes in the foreign currency system.
"There is no change in the exchange rate system," Meridor said after a meeting with Frenkel.
Frenkel vowed to continue to defend the exchange rate even though that has forced the central bank to inject more than an estimated $1 billion during January intervening in the market.

"The Bank of Israel will continue to defend the system," he said. "We have all the tools required to do this and we will continue to do so. Every dollar the Bank of Israel buys and the shekels we consequently sell we are absorbing immediately."
The shekel traded quietly on Tuesday and the Bank of Israel did not intervene in the local foreign currency market.

Since mid-January, the shekel has been trading at the bottom end of its trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is pegged. To prevent it from sliding under the band, the Bank of Israel has been intervening heavily in the local currency market.

The financial daily Globes quoted senior central bank officials as saying they were considering various measures to alleviate pressure on the Bank of Israel to support the exchange rate and absorb the liquidity created by intervention.

Among them was a special tax on short-term foreign currency borrowing; widening the trading band, which now allows the shekel to deviate up to seven percent above or below a sloping rate to as much as 12 percent; suspending further government borrowing overseas; and increasing the reserve requirement by five percentage points.
Frenkel expressed concern about the unexpectedly wide budget deficit in January, which reached 1.28 billion shekels.

"When in January the budget figures are so worrisome following so great an effort by the government (to approve the 1997 budget), it is very important that the budget cut which was decided upon is in fact implemented," Frenkel said.
"What happened in January is a result that troubles us very much," he said.
